You typed something, deleted it, and then hit undo and it came back. How does the app know what to undo? It does not just remember the result. It remembers the action itself as an object.
That is exactly what the Command Pattern does.
Instead of calling a method directly, you wrap the request in an object a command. That command knows what to do, who to do it to, and how to undo it.
Without Command Pattern:
The sender has to know everything about the receiver. Want to undo? Add undo logic everywhere. Want to queue actions? No way. Want to log every action? Good luck.
With Command Pattern:
Each action is now a self-contained object. You can execute it, undo it, queue it, log it, or replay it without the sender knowing anything about the receiver.
It is useful when:
["You need undo and redo functionality.","You want to queue or schedule actions.","You want to log every operation that happens.","You want to decouple who triggers an action from who performs it."]

blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Tightly Coupled Restaurant Order System
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Tightly Coupled Restaurant Order System

blocks.content: Imagine you are building a restaurant management system. The system needs to send orders to different stations the kitchen, the bar, and the dessert counter.
Naive Implementation
Why This Design Fails
1. Tight Coupling WaiterNaive directly knows about every station Kitchen, Bar, and DessertCounter. Add a new station like a Grill Counter and you must modify the waiter class again.
2. Poor Scalability Every new station means new fields, new methods, and a bigger class. The waiter ends up knowing about every single thing happening in the restaurant.

3. No Undo Support Customer wants to cancel an order? You would have to manually track every order placed, write custom cancellation logic for each station, and add if-else blocks to figure out what to reverse.
4. No Queuing or Scheduling Want to delay an order or queue it for rush hour? Impossible actions are hardcoded method calls, not objects you can store and fire later.

5. No Reusable Actions If the same "cook pasta" order needs to come from a waiter, a mobile app, and a self-service kiosk each one needs its own direct coupling to Kitchen. The action cannot be passed around independently.
What We Really Need

Each order"cook pasta", "prepare juice", "serve cake" should be a standalone object that knows what to do, which station handles it, how to execute it, and how to cancel it. The waiter should not care how an order works. They just deliver it.
This is exactly what the Command Pattern enables.
2. What is the Command Pattern?

The Command Pattern turns a request into a standalone object containing everything needed to perform that request. This lets you queue requests, delay execution, log every action, and support undo all without the sender knowing anything about the receiver.
Two things define it:

1. Requests become objects Each action cook a meal, prepare a drink, serve dessert becomes its own object implementing a common interface. The object holds a reference to the receiver and knows exactly how to execute and undo the action.

2. Invoker and receiver are decoupled The waiter does not know how the kitchen cooks. The kitchen does not know who placed the order. The command object sits between them and handles the translation completely.

Real-World Analogy

Think about ordering food at a restaurant.

You tell the waiter what you want. The waiter writes it on an order slip. The waiter does not cook the food they carry the slip to the kitchen. The chef reads the slip and prepares the dish.

  • The order slip is the Command object
  • The waiter is the Invoker carries and delivers the request
  • The chef is the Receiver does the actual work
  • The customer is the Client creates the request

The waiter does not need to know how to cook. The chef does not need to know who ordered. The slip decouples them completely.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245808880-d8c41ede.png
The Four Participants
Command Interface Declares execute() and undo() that every command must implement. The invoker only ever sees this interface never the concrete commands or receivers.

ConcreteCommand CookMealCommand, PrepareDrinkCommand Each implements the Command interface and bridges the gap between the waiter and a specific station. Stores a reference to its receiver and delegates all real work to it.
Receiver Kitchen, Bar, DessertCounter The stations that do the actual work. They know how to cook, mix, and plate but have zero knowledge of commands or the waiter. Plain domain objects.
Invoker Waiter Triggers command execution. Does not know what any command does or which station handles it. Just calls execute() and maintains a history stack for undo.
3. How It Works
Here is the Command Pattern workflow step by step:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245809112-a73690db.png

Step 1: Client creates receivers and commands The client creates the station objects Kitchen, Bar, DessertCounter and wraps each action in a command object, passing the appropriate receiver to each command.
Step 2: Client configures the invoker The client hands command objects to the Waiter. The waiter never knows which station handles what it just holds commands.
Step 3: User triggers the invoker When an order is placed, the waiter calls execute() on the command. It has no idea what happens next it just calls the interface method.
Step 4: Command delegates to the receiver The concrete command's execute() calls the right method on its receiver. CookMealCommand calls kitchen.cookMeal(). The receiver does the actual work.
Step 5: Invoker records the command in history After successful execution the waiter pushes the command onto a history stack for potential cancellation.
Step 6: User triggers undo The waiter pops the most recent command from the stack and calls undo(). The command tells the station to reverse the action.
4. Implementing Command Pattern
Let's refactor the restaurant system using the Command Pattern with full undo support.
Step 1: Define the Command Interface
Step 2: Define the Receivers
The actual stations that do the real work. They have zero knowledge of commands or the waiter.
Step 3: Implement Concrete Commands
Each command wraps one receiver action. For simple orders undo just calls the cancel method. Notice how the command handles all the reversal logic the waiter never needs to know any of this.
Step 4: Create the Invoker with Undo Support
blocks.text: Step 4: Create the Invoker with Undo Support

blocks.content: The Waiter is the invoker. It accepts any command, executes it, and maintains a history stack for undo. It never knows what the commands do or which station they talk to.

The Waiter is clean and focused. It does not import Kitchen, Bar, or DessertCounter. It only depends on the Command interface. Adding a hundred new stations does not require changing a single line here.

5. Practical Example: Shopping Cart with Undo/Redo
blocks.text: 5. Practical Example: Shopping Cart with Undo/Redo

blocks.content: Let's apply the Command Pattern to a shopping cart. The cart supports adding items, removing items, and applying discounts. All operations are undoable and redoable using a two-stack approach.

blocks.content: A few things to notice. First, redo works correctly after undoing the keyboard addition, redoing brings it back by re-executing the sameAddItemCommand.

Second,ApplyDiscountCommandsaves nothing during construction it calculates and reverses the discount mathematically. Third, performing a new action after undoing clears the redo stack this is standard undo/redo behavior, a new action creates a new timeline.
